faq.q: Why are carbon fibre layers laid in different directions?
faq.a: A carbon fibre is very strong along its length but weak across it. Stacking layers at 0, 45 and 90 degrees gives strength in every direction the part will be loaded, such as pulling, bending and twisting.
asks: What does the weave direction in carbon fibre do?

faq.q: Why is carbon fibre baked under vacuum?
faq.a: Sucking the air out presses the layers tightly together and removes bubbles, which would be weak spots. Heat and pressure in an autoclave then cure the resin so the part comes out dense and strong.
A composite combines two materials to get the best of both. In carbon fibre composite, stiff, strong fibres carry the load, and the resin holds them in place and shares the load between them.

faq.q: Why is carbon fibre so light and strong?
faq.a: Carbon atoms in the fibres are bonded in long, strong chains of sheets, and carbon is a light element. The composite weighs about a fifth as much as steel for the same size, yet can be as stiff.
asks: Is carbon fibre stronger than steel?

faq.q: Why is carbon fibre so expensive?
faq.a: Making the fibres takes lots of energy, heating plastic fibres to over 1,000 degrees Celsius without oxygen, and parts are often laid up by hand and cured for hours. That is why it is used mostly in racing cars, aircraft, bikes and sports gear.
asks: Why don't all cars use carbon fibre?

facts: Most carbon fibre is made by heating acrylic (polyacrylonitrile) fibres to over 1,000 °C without oxygen.
Carbon fibre composite weighs roughly a fifth as much as steel for the same volume.
